You've identified a powerful underlying principle! XOR operations have a unique property: when you apply XOR between identical values, they cancel each other out, leaving only the unique or "extra" value.

Conceptually, if you XOR all characters from both s and t together (t contains every letter from s, but with one additional letter), the result will isolate that one added character. This is because each matching character pair between s and t vanishes under XOR, and only the unpaired (new) letter remains.

This type of insight is valued both in algorithm design and technical interviews, as it reveals a deep understanding of how bitwise operations can be used for set difference or matching problems.
